title: Central tendency and dispersion
summary: The [[mean|mean]], [[median|median]] and [[mode|mode]] describe the centre of a data set. The [[interquartile-range|interquartile range]] and [[standard-deviation|standard deviation]] describe its spread. You find each for lists, tables and grouped data, and see what shifting or scaling the data does.

goals.text: Find the mean, median and mode of a list or a frequency table, by formula and with your GDC.
Estimate the mean of grouped data from [[mid-interval-value|mid-interval values]], and find the [[modal-class|modal class]].
Find quartiles and the IQR by hand and with your GDC, and explain why the two can differ.
Find the standard deviation and [[variance|variance]] with your GDC, and say what they measure.
Say how adding to or multiplying every value changes the mean and standard deviation.

synonyms: effect of adding a constant on the mean

before.prompt: How many of these $20$ students own fewer than $2$ pets? $\begin{array}{c|cccc} \text{pets} & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 \\ \hline f & 5 & 8 & 4 & 3 \end{array}$
before.explain: $5 + 8 = 13$: a cumulative frequency. Revise it in {{lesson:4.2}}.

before.prompt: Masses, $m$ grams, are grouped as $40 \le m < 50$, $50 \le m < 60$ and $60 \le m < 70$. Which class holds a mass of exactly $60$ g?
before.hint: Which class includes its left end?

options.text: Neither: $60$ is a boundary, so it is left out

before.explain: $60 \le m < 70$ includes $60$; $50 \le m < 60$ stops just below it. Revise it in {{lesson:4.2}}.

before.prompt: A box and whisker diagram has minimum $8$, $Q_{1} = 14$, median $19$, $Q_{3} = 25$ and maximum $40$. What percentage of the data lies between $14$ and $25$?
before.hint: The box runs from one quartile to the other.
before.explain: The box holds the middle half of the data, from $Q_{1}$ to $Q_{3}$. Revise it in {{lesson:4.2}}.

blocks.text: Nine students score $2, 5, 1, 4, 3, 4, 0, 4, 4$ on a $5$-question quiz. What is a typical score? Three different averages answer this.

blocks.statement: The [[mean|mean]] of $n$ values is their total divided by $n$: $\bar{x} = \frac{\sum x}{n}$, where $\sum x$ (sigma $x$) is the total.
blocks.plain: Share the total out equally between the values.

blocks.statement: The [[median|median]] is the middle value of the ordered data: the $\frac{n+1}{2}$th value. For even $n$, average the two middle values.
blocks.plain: Half the data lie at or below it, and half at or above it.

blocks.statement: The [[mode|mode]] is the value that occurs most often. A data set can have more than one mode.

blocks.question: Find the mean, median and mode of the quiz scores $2, 5, 1, 4, 3, 4, 0, 4, 4$.
steps: Mean: the total is $27$ and $n = 9$, so $\bar{x} = \frac{27}{9} = 3$.
Median: in order, $0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 4, 4, 4, 5$. The median is the $\frac{9 + 1}{2} = 5$th value, $4$.
Mode: $4$ appears four times, more than any other score.
The low scores $0$ and $1$ pull the mean below the median.

blocks.text: In a frequency table, each value $x_{i}$ appears $f_{i}$ times, so it adds $f_{i}x_{i}$ to the total. This formula is in the formula booklet.
Here $k$ is the number of different values. The total frequency $n$ counts data values, not columns.

blocks.question: The number of people, $x$, in each of $30$ cars at a checkpoint is shown. $\begin{array}{c|ccccc} x & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 \\ \hline f & 14 & 9 & 4 & 2 & 1 \end{array}$ Find the mean, median and mode of $x$.
steps: Median: with $n = 30$, average the $15$th and $16$th values. The first $14$ values are $1$, and the $15$th to $23$rd are $2$.
So the $15$th and $16$th values are both $2$, and the median is $2$.
Mode: $x = 1$ has the highest frequency, $14$.

blocks.text: Taking the middle column, $x = 3$, as the median. Count through the frequencies to find the middle data value.
On Paper 2, your GDC finds the mean from a list of values and a list of frequencies (keystrokes in the next section).

blocks.hint: Order the values first. There is an even number of them.
blocks.explain: In order: $7, 9, 10, 12, 15, 18$. The middle two are $10$ and $12$, so the median is $11$.

blocks.prompt: Find the mean of $x$. $\begin{array}{c|cccc} x & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 \\ \hline f & 4 & 7 & 6 & 3 \end{array}$
blocks.hint: Find $\sum f_{i}x_{i}$, then divide by the total frequency.
blocks.explain: $\sum f_{i}x_{i} = 28$ and $n = 20$, so $\bar{x} = 1.4$. Dividing $28$ by the $4$ columns gives $7$, which is wrong.

blocks.prompt: The mean of $8$ numbers is $6$. A ninth number is added, and the mean of all nine is $7$. Find the ninth number.
blocks.hint: Turn each mean into a total, using total $= n \times \bar{x}$.
blocks.explain: The totals are $9 \times 7 = 63$ and $8 \times 6 = 48$, so the ninth number is $63 - 48 = 15$.

blocks.text: Sometimes you only know which class each value is in. Then you can't find the exact [[mean|mean]], but you can estimate it.
The idea: treat every value in a class as if it sat at the middle of the class.

blocks.statement: The [[mid-interval-value|mid-interval value]] of the class $a \le x < b$ is $\frac{a + b}{2}$.
blocks.plain: The point halfway along the class.

blocks.text: Use the booklet formula with each $x_{i}$ a mid-interval value. The result is an estimate, not the exact mean.

blocks.statement: When the classes have equal widths, the [[modal-class|modal class]] is the class with the highest frequency.

blocks.question: The journey times, $t$ minutes, of $40$ commuters are shown. $\begin{array}{c|c} t & f \\ \hline 0 \le t < 10 & 6 \\ 10 \le t < 20 & 15 \\ 20 \le t < 30 & 11 \\ 30 \le t < 40 & 8 \end{array}$ (a) Write down the modal class. (b) Find an estimate of the mean journey time.
steps: (a) The classes have equal widths, and the highest frequency is $15$. So the modal class is $10 \le t < 20$.
(b) The mid-interval values are $5$, $15$, $25$ and $35$.
$\sum f_{i}x_{i} = 6 \times 5 + 15 \times 15 + 11 \times 25 + 8 \times 35 = 810$.
The estimated mean is $\frac{810}{40} = 20.25$ minutes, which sits among the busiest classes.

blocks.text: Using a class boundary, such as $10$ or $20$, as the value for a class. Use the mid-interval value, here $15$.

blocks.question: The masses, $m$ grams, of $60$ apples are shown. $\begin{array}{c|c} m & f \\ \hline 80 \le m < 100 & 5 \\ 100 \le m < 120 & 13 \\ 120 \le m < 140 & 21 \\ 140 \le m < 160 & 14 \\ 160 \le m < 180 & 7 \end{array}$ Use your calculator to find an estimate of the mean mass. Give your answer to 3 s.f.
steps: Put the mid-interval values $90, 110, 130, 150, 170$ into one list, with the frequencies $5, 13, 21, 14, 7$ beside them. Write both lists in your answer: that earns the method mark.
Run one-variable statistics with the frequency list attached. Check that $n = 60$: if it shows $5$, the frequencies are missing.
Read off $\bar{x} = 131.666\ldots$, and round only now.

blocks.text: Estimate is a command term. Use mid-interval values, and call your answer an estimate.

blocks.prompt: Find an estimate of the mean of $x$. $\begin{array}{c|c} x & f \\ \hline 0 \le x < 4 & 3 \\ 4 \le x < 8 & 5 \\ 8 \le x < 12 & 2 \end{array}$
What is the modal class of these seedling heights, $h$ cm? $\begin{array}{c|c} h & f \\ \hline 10 \le h < 20 & 7 \\ 20 \le h < 30 & 12 \\ 30 \le h < 40 & 15 \\ 40 \le h < 50 & 6 \end{array}$
blocks.hint: The answer is a class, not a single number.
blocks.explain: The highest frequency, $15$, is in $30 \le h < 40$. Give the class, not its frequency or its mid-interval value.

blocks.text: A measure of [[dispersion|dispersion]] says how spread out the data are.
The simplest is the range, largest value minus smallest. One unusual value can change it a lot.

blocks.statement: With the data in order, the lower [[quartile|quartile]] $Q_{1}$ has a quarter of the values below it. The upper quartile $Q_{3}$ has three quarters below it.
blocks.plain: The quartiles and the median cut the ordered data into four equal parts.

blocks.text: 1. To find the quartiles by hand, order the data and find the [[median|median]].
2. Split the data into a lower half and an upper half. When $n$ is odd, leave the median out of both halves.
3. $Q_{1}$ is the median of the lower half, and $Q_{3}$ is the median of the upper half.
The [[interquartile-range|interquartile range]] (IQR) is the spread of the middle half of the data, so extreme values don't affect it. It is in the booklet.

blocks.question: The ages of the $11$ members of a choir are $34, 19, 52, 41, 27, 63, 45, 38, 29, 56, 47$. Find $Q_{1}$, $Q_{3}$ and the interquartile range.
steps: In order: $19, 27, 29, 34, 38, 41, 45, 47, 52, 56, 63$. The median is the $6$th value, $41$; leave it out of both halves.
$\mathrm{IQR} = 52 - 29 = 23$ years.

blocks.text: Other methods exist: some keep the median in both halves, and spreadsheets often interpolate. So the same data can give slightly different quartiles.

Your GDC uses one fixed method. In their usual settings, the three models in these notes leave the median out when $n$ is odd, as above. A by-hand answer can differ from the GDC's, and each is right for its method.

blocks.question: The numbers of goals, $x$, in $40$ football matches are shown. $\begin{array}{c|cccccc} x & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 \\ \hline f & 7 & 11 & 9 & 7 & 4 & 2 \end{array}$ (a) Use your calculator to find $Q_{1}$ and $Q_{3}$. (b) Show that the data have no outliers.
steps: (a) Enter $0$ to $5$ and the frequencies as in the apple example, and run one-variable statistics. Write down $Q_{1} = 1$ and $Q_{3} = 3$.
Check $Q_{1}$ by counting: the $10$th and $11$th values are both $1$.
(b) Use the rule from {{lesson:4.1}}. $\mathrm{IQR} = 2$, so the fences are $1 - 1.5 \times 2 = -2$ and $3 + 1.5 \times 2 = 6$.
All values lie from $0$ to $5$, inside the fences, so there are no outliers.

blocks.text: Write the GDC's quartiles down before using them: later parts can then earn follow-through (FT) marks even if one is wrong.
Giving the range when asked for the IQR. Subtract the quartiles, not the smallest value from the largest.

blocks.hint: Each half has $4$ values. Find the median of each half.

blocks.prompt: For the data $2, 4, 5, 7, 11$, a student keeps the median in both halves and gets $Q_{1} = 4$. Her GDC gives $Q_{1} = 3$. Which statement is correct?
blocks.hint: Find the lower half twice: once with the median, once without.

options.text: She made an arithmetic slip, so $Q_{1} = 3$
They use different methods, and each value is right for its method

blocks.explain: With the median, the lower half is $2, 4, 5$, so $Q_{1} = 4$. Without it, the lower half is $2, 4$, so $Q_{1} = 3$. Both methods are in use.

blocks.text: The [[interquartile-range|IQR]] uses only the [[quartile|quartiles]]. The [[standard-deviation|standard deviation]] uses every value: it measures how far the values typically lie from the [[mean|mean]].

blocks.alt: Two dot plots on the same scale from 4 to 16. Set A has six dots close together, at 8, 9, 10, 10, 11 and 12. Set B has six dots spread out, at 4, 6, 10, 10, 14 and 16. A dashed line marks the mean, 10, of both sets.
blocks.caption: Both sets have mean $10$. Set B's values lie further from the mean, so its standard deviation is larger: about $4.16$, against $1.29$.

blocks.statement: The standard deviation $\sigma$ measures the typical distance of the values from the mean. The [[variance|variance]] is its square, $\sigma^{2}$.
blocks.plain: A small standard deviation means the values huddle close to the mean.

blocks.text: In the exam you find $\sigma$ with your GDC only. One small case by hand shows what it means: the variance is the mean of the squared distances from the mean, $\sigma^{2} = \frac{\sum (x - \bar{x})^{2}}{n}$.

blocks.question: Find the variance and the standard deviation of $2, 4, 4, 5, 10$ by hand.
steps: Mean: $\bar{x} = \frac{25}{5} = 5$.
Distances from the mean: $-3, -1, -1, 0, 5$. They add up to $0$, so square them first.
$\sigma = \sqrt{7.2} = 2.683\ldots$.

blocks.text: Your GDC shows two standard deviations. In IB Maths AA you use $\sigma_{x}$, which divides by $n$ as above. Ignore $s_{x}$, which divides by $n - 1$.

blocks.question: The number of eggs, $x$, in each of $40$ nests is shown. $\begin{array}{c|cccccc} x & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 & 6 \\ \hline f & 4 & 9 & 13 & 8 & 4 & 2 \end{array}$ Use your calculator to find (a) the mean; (b) the standard deviation; (c) the variance.
steps: Enter $1$ to $6$ and the frequencies, run one-variable statistics and check that $n = 40$.
(a) $\bar{x} = 3.125$. This is exact, so give it as it is.
(b) $\sigma_{x} = 1.28816\ldots$, so $\sigma \approx 1.29$.
(c) Square the unrounded value: $(1.28816\ldots)^{2} = 1.659375$, so $\sigma^{2} \approx 1.66$.

blocks.text: Quoting $s_{x}$ from the GDC. The standard deviation you need is $\sigma_{x}$.

blocks.prompt: Use your calculator to find the standard deviation of $3, 5, 7, 9$.
blocks.hint: Use the GDC value that divides by $n$.
blocks.explain: $\sigma_{x} = \sqrt{5} \approx 2.24$. The value $2.58$ is $s_{x}$, and $5$ is the variance.

blocks.prompt: Ana's $400$ m times have mean $58.2$ s and standard deviation $0.6$ s. Bea's have mean $57.9$ s and standard deviation $1.4$ s. Which is correct?
blocks.hint: A lower mean time is faster. A smaller standard deviation means more consistent.

options.text: Ana is faster on average and more consistent
Bea is faster on average and more consistent
Bea is faster on average, but Ana is more consistent

blocks.explain: Bea's lower mean means she is faster on average. Ana's smaller standard deviation means her times vary less.

sections.heading: Adding to or scaling every value

blocks.text: Add $5$ marks to every test score. Every score, and so the [[mean|mean]], moves up by $5$. The gaps between scores don't change, so the spread doesn't either.
Double every score instead. Every score and every gap doubles, so the mean and the [[standard-deviation|standard deviation]] both double.

blocks.statement: If every value $x$ becomes $ax + b$, where $a > 0$, the new mean is $a\bar{x} + b$ and the new standard deviation is $a\sigma$. The new [[variance|variance]] is $a^{2}\sigma^{2}$.
blocks.why: Adding $b$ slides the data without changing any gap; multiplying by $a$ stretches every distance from the mean by $a$.

blocks.text: $b$ can be negative: subtracting $4$ from every value lowers the mean by $4$ and leaves $\sigma$ unchanged. The [[median|median]], [[quartile|quartiles]] and mode change like the mean; the [[interquartile-range|IQR]] and range change like $\sigma$.

blocks.question: One June, a town's daily maximum temperatures have mean $18.5$ and standard deviation $3.2$, in degrees Celsius. They are converted to degrees Fahrenheit using $F = 1.8C + 32$. Find (a) the mean, (b) the standard deviation and (c) the variance in degrees Fahrenheit.
steps: Every value is multiplied by $a = 1.8$, then $b = 32$ is added.
(b) The $+32$ has no effect on the spread, so $\sigma_{F} = 1.8 \times 3.2 = 5.76$.
(c) $\sigma_{F}^{2} = 5.76^{2} = 33.1776 \approx 33.2$. This equals $1.8^{2} \times 3.2^{2}$: the $1.8$ is squared too.

blocks.question: A data set has mean $12$ and standard deviation $2.5$. Every value $x$ is changed to $ax + b$, where $a > 0$. The new mean is $50$ and the new standard deviation is $10$. Find $a$ and $b$.
steps: Only $a$ affects the standard deviation: $2.5a = 10$, so $a = 4$.
Both affect the mean: $12a + b = 50$, so $48 + b = 50$ and $b = 2$.
Check: $4 \times 12 + 2 = 50$ and $4 \times 2.5 = 10$.

blocks.text: Adding $b$ to the standard deviation too. Shifting the data leaves $\sigma$ unchanged.
At HL the same rules apply to random variables: $\mathrm{E}(aX + b) = a\mathrm{E}(X) + b$ and $\mathrm{Var}(aX + b) = a^{2}\mathrm{Var}(X)$.

blocks.prompt: The ages of a club's members have standard deviation $7.3$ years. Find the standard deviation of their ages in $5$ years' time.
blocks.hint: Every age goes up by the same amount.
blocks.explain: Adding $5$ to every age shifts the data without changing the gaps, so $\sigma$ is still $7.3$ years.

blocks.prompt: A data set has variance $9$. Every value is multiplied by $3$. Find the new variance.
blocks.hint: Find the standard deviation first, then multiply it by $3$.
blocks.explain: $\sigma$ goes from $3$ to $9$, so the variance goes from $9$ to $81$: it is multiplied by $3^{2}$.

blocks.text: Median: the $\frac{n+1}{2}$th value in order; for even $n$, the mean of the middle two. Mode: the most frequent value.
Grouped data: estimate the mean with mid-interval values $\frac{a+b}{2}$. The modal class has the highest frequency.
Quartiles: medians of the lower and upper halves, median left out when $n$ is odd. Other methods may differ slightly.
Standard deviation: GDC only, using $\sigma_{x}$, not $s_{x}$. Variance $= \sigma^{2}$: square the unrounded value.
$x \to ax + b$ with $a > 0$: mean $\to a\bar{x} + b$, $\sigma \to a\sigma$, variance $\to a^{2}\sigma^{2}$.

mistakes: Taking one of the middle two values, or the middle column of a table, as the median. For even $n$, average the middle two data values.
Dividing $\sum f_{i}x_{i}$ by the number of columns. Divide by the total frequency $n$.
Using class boundaries instead of mid-interval values, or leaving the frequency list off on the GDC. Check that the GDC shows the right $n$.
Quoting $s_{x}$ from the GDC as the standard deviation. In IB Maths AA you use $\sigma_{x}$.
Multiplying the variance by $a$, or adding $b$ to $\sigma$. Under $ax + b$, $\sigma$ becomes $a\sigma$ and the variance $a^{2}\sigma^{2}$.
examTips: Write down the mode or median: no working needed. Find the mean: show $\frac{\sum f_{i}x_{i}}{n}$ with your numbers in, for the method mark.
On Paper 2, write down the lists you entered before the GDC's answer.
Round only the final answer, to 3 s.f. unless the question asks for another precision, such as 4 s.f.
